text: Carbocations are highly important reactive intermediates in organic chemistry. They are often high energy/reactive and their formation are likely the rate-determining step in many reactions.

Their stability is therefore often related to the reaction kinetics. The more stable the carbocation, the faster the mechanistic pathway where it is formed, compared to those of alternative carbocations. Adjacent group which can donate electrons through inductive effect, conjugation or hyperconjugation all stabilise carbocations.
There are three main types of reactions a carbocations can undergo:
1. Reacting with a nucleophile to form a new bond.
2. Losing a proton (mind the charges!) at the next carbon (beta position) to form a C=C bond.
3. Rearrange to a more stable carbocation.
Or sometimes, a combination of all three can happen in a highly efficient cascade reaction to give many changes between the starting material and the product.

questions.explanation: A carbocation can react with a nucleophile, lose a proton at the beta position to form a C=C bond, or rearrange to a more stable carbocation. In this reaction, there is no proton at the beta positions to lose, and no thermodynamic drive for a rearrangement. However, the allylic cation can have two resonance forms, giving us to two position for the nucleophile to attack. We also have two nucleophiles, Cl- and H2O (formed in the generation of the carbocation), so there are 3 possible products and the reforming of the starting material. Admittedly, C is less likely than the others mainly due to the low concentration of H2O.

questions.explanation: This is a Beckmann rearrangement with the OH on the N atom pointing away from the more hindered side of the imine. As a rule, rearrangements can be confusing and it is easy to make mistakes with the structures. The two key strategies to deal with this are: (i) do not move the non-H atoms; and (ii) use numbering to track all your atoms and bonds between them. In this example, one can number the ring and the N atom from 1 to 8 in the clock-wise direction. The curly arrows indicate breaking the bond between 8 and 2, and forming a new bond between 8 and 1. So in the product, without moving any C or N atom, we simply make those changes. The methyl group on atom number 8 is reproduced in the product, without any change to its stereochemistry. Now we have the correct product, albeit terribly drawn. The final step is to redraw it according to the convention. Again, this can be error prone and the numbering helps in checking if any mistake is made. NOTE: Do not add one atom, or remove one, in your answer. Too many of these in the exam! Once the correct rearranged product is drawn, the rest of the mechanism follows the standard steps to give the cyclic amide.

A bond is broken between 2 and 6, and is replaced with a new bond between 6 and 1. After the rearrangement, since there is no good nucleophile, the only option left is to eliminate a proton to form the double bond. The correct one (red curly arrows) is the one which generates the most stable carbocation (i.e. stabilised by the lone pair on the adjacent oxygen, and requires the migration of the most labile group (i.e. the CH2-O- group). The rest of the mechanism is simply the lost of a proton to generate the ketone product. The easiest way to make a mistake here is to lose track of the various stereochemical centres.

text: Three sub-topics were covered this during lectures: acid/base catalysis, nucleophilic catalysis and enzyme catalysis. The salient points are summarised below. They are general vs specific acid/base catalysis, how nucleophilic catalysis work, and how both of these combine in enzyme catalysis.

questions.question_text: Should a reaction following general acid catalysis mechanism be performed at lower or higher temperature?
questions.explanation: This is a complex question, as the reaction rate tends to be faster at higher temperature due to the Ahrenius equation. However, the negative delta entropy of activation of general acid catalysis mean that the increase in reaction rate will be less compared to other reactions. This is particularly important if there is a competing reaction with positive delta entropy of activation. Lowering the temperature in this case will slow down the desired reaction less than it would the undesired reaction, thus it will improve the selectivity.

questions.question_text: Is the reaction below a general or specific base catalysis case?
questions.explanation: The pKa value of the alcohol is much higher than that of the K3PO4 base in water. Even if the gap narrows in organic solvents, it is unlikely that the phosphate can deprotonate the alcohol outright. Thus, this is a general base catalysis case under the forth bullet point: Catalyst too weak to deprotonate reagent. NOTE: In this particular case, the K3PO4 acts as both a general base catalyst and a reagent, ultimately consumed to quench the proton generated by the balanced equation.

questions.question_text: Which is the best catalyst for this reaction under specific acid catalysis mechanism?
questions.explanation: For a specific acid catalysis mechanism, the strength of the acid is important as it influence the concentration of the active species through protonation equilibrium. Thus, the strongest acid will result in the fastest reaction. HCl will be the best choice in this case.

The additional substituents can cause confusion, but the core change is the same as with all Baylis-Hillman reactions. One way to navigate through this type of questions is with some assistance from drawing the mechanism, although one doesn't need to draw out all the steps.

questions.question_text: Draw the product of this reaction:
questions.explanation: This is a more difficult question. There are two enones, which can confuse the issue. The catalyst is still DABCO, so we're looking at a nucleophilic catalysis case, maybe a variation of Baylis-Hillman reaction. When confronted with this type of question, you should have confidence that the new reaction will be built on similar fundamental steps to those you have seeen before. Starting with DABCO's 1,4-addition to the enone, the first question is which enone? Of of the two, the ketone is the more electron poor electrophile and should be the preferred target. This makes the ester the electrophile target for the enolate intermediate. Attack on the ester will be less likely (both electronically and sterically) compared to a SN2 on the C atom with the bromide leaving group.

questions.question_text: Can you suggest a suitable catalyst for this reaction?
questions.explanation: This is a classic case of nucleophilic catalysis. Any catalyst which is a good nucleophile and can act as a good leaving group from the intermediate is eligible. Thus, the correct answer is all of them.

questions.question_text: Are the three amino acids below a valid catalytic triad in an enzyme?
questions.explanation: The standard catalytic triad have a Ser residue at the position of the Lys residue in this triad. Ser-OH can be activated through general base catalysis by the imidazole on His, allowing it to attack as a nucleophile. At pH 7.4, the -NH2 group of the Lys residue will be protonated, and cannot act as a nucleophile. Thus, the correct answer is No.

questions.question_text: What is the role of NADH in enzymatic reactions?
questions.explanation: NADH and NADPH are common enzyme co-factor in biological system. They typically acts as a reductant, taking in an electron, and delivering a hydride to the substrate. Thus, the correct answer is all of them.

questions.question_text: What are the common limitations of enzyme catalysis?
options: They cannot work in organic solvents, leading to problems with solubility of substrates.
They normally only works under relatively neutral conditions.
They often require co-factors, which can significantly reduce their green impacts.
questions.explanation: While natural enzymes evolved to work in water, enzymes can be modified to work in organic solvents through directed evolution. This is a costly process, but modern synthetic processes have started incorporating enzymatic processes in organic solvents on scale.

text: This section covers the reactivity and reactions of carbenes and nitrenes. They will be divided into:
(i) Cyclopropanation under thermal and photochemical conditions.
(ii) C-H insertion and its selectivity.
(iii) Curtius rearrangement and its use in ring expansion.

The key point is that a carbene has 6 electrons on the carbon atom. In its singlet state, the reactive centre has one pair of electron and one empty orbital to form two new bonds in a synchronous manner. These can be two new sigma bonds, leading to either a cyclopropane (in a reaction with a C=C bond) or a new -C-C-H moiety (in a reaction with a weaker C-H bond).

Under photochemical conditions, the carbene can be excited into a triplet, with two unpaired electrons in two different orbitals. This species will form two new bonds (using half arrows!) in asynchronous manner, i.e. step-wise.

questions.question_text: Draw the product of this reaction, paying attention to its stereochemistry:
questions.explanation: This is a cyclopropanation under thermal conditions. The carbene will be a singlet and the two bonds will be formed together. Thus, the stereochemistry of the C=C bond is retained in the product, give a trans substitution pattern in the product.

questions.question_text: Which are the possible products of this reaction?
questions.explanation: This is a cyclopropanation under photochemical conditions. The carbene will be a triplet and the two bonds will be formed in a step-wise manner. Thus, the stereochemistry of the C=C bond is lost in the product, give no control of the stereochemistry of the product. All three stereoisomers (RR, SS and RS) are possible products.

questions.question_text: Which is the best disconnection to make the cyclopropane below?
questions.explanation: The best disconnection should result in starting materials which are readily made or commercially available. It should also avoid any selectivity issue in the forward reaction, e.g. competing functional groups which can react, regio- and stereoselectivity. This doesn't mean that there must be no selectivity to be considered, but rather that the selectivity should be obvious and overwhelmingly favouring the desired product. Thus, the three disconnections must be assessed based on these criteria.

C1 is next to the benzene ring, which destabilises the C-H bond through hyperconjugation. Thus, this is the preferred position for the C-H insertion.

text: Free radicals are species with unpaired electrons. In organic chemistry, we mostly focus on C-centred radicals, with 7 electrons on the carbon atoms. Here are some of the key points to remember:
1. Oxygen is a diradical, which can quench radical reactions. So in pratice, one has to degass the solution before stating a radical reaction.

2. A free radical reaction needs an initiator, which contains a weak bond which can undergo homolytic cleavage under thermal or photochemical conditions. Controlling the concentration of radical initiator is critical to keeping the reaction going to completion within a reasonable timescale.
3. Once formed, the radical from the initiator can react with the first substrate, generating the first working radical. This is the end of initiation, leading to the propagation steps.

4. In propagation steps, the first working radical undergos reactions with other substrate, leading to the products and regeneration of this radical. This allows the propagation steps to happen over and over again, until the termination which destroy the radicals.

5. The termination steps are any coming together between two radicals, forming a new bond. These take out free radicals from the system, and stopping the propagation steps and the overall reaction. This is exactly how radical scavengers, which are stable radicals themselves, work.

6. For propagation steps, a free radical can (i) abstract an atom from another molecule, forming a new stable bond and another radical (as with Bu3Sn. reacting with Br-CR3 to form Bu3Sn-Br and R3C.), or (ii) reacting with a pi bond in a addition reaction (e-rich radicals prefer e-poor pi bonds and e-poor radicals prefer e-rich pi bonds), forming a new C-C bond and a new radical.
7. Lastly, radical reaction mechanisms are drawn with half arrows representing the movement of a single electron.

questions.question_text: Which of these are possible radical reaction initiator?
questions.explanation: A radical initiator is a compound which contains a weak bond which undergo homolytic breakage upon heating, giving free radicals which can start the reaction. Using correctly, they replenish the free radicals in the reaction, due to termination bond formation between two random free radicals, and keep it going. B is out, as it is a free radical (it actually acts as a radical scavenger). D doesn't have a weak bond which can undergo homolytic cleavage. Both A and C qualify as initiators for radical reactions.

questions.question_text: Is this bromination reaction following a radical or ionic mechanism?
questions.explanation: Bromination can happen through both radical and ionic mechanisms. The clues to tell them apart often come from the solvent (polar solvent suggesting ionic mechanism), the acidic or basic conditions (both supporting an ionic mechanism), and the present of a radical initiator or photochemical conditions (suggesting free radical mechanism). The reason we care is because the two types of mechanism have different selectivities. In this case, the presence of AIBN as a radical initiator is telling.

questions.question_text: Which of these are/is a stable free radical?
questions.explanation: A, B and D are all intermediates in previously shown free radical reaction mechanisms. Thus, they are not stable free radicals. Instead they're reactive. The only option left is C. The radical is stabilised by conjugation with the lone pair on N atom, and prevented from easily reacting with other reactants by steric hindrance from 4 Me groups in adjacent carbon atoms. Hence, this is a stable free radical (TEMPO, commercially sold by many chemical suppliers).

questions.question_text: Which is the major product of the following reaction?
questions.explanation: This is a free radical polymerisation. The two substrates are opposite in electronic properties. One is e-rich and the other is e-poor. As e-poor radicals prefer to react with e-rich C=C bonds, and e-rich radicals prefer to react with e-poor C=C, the product should be the perfectly alternating co-polymer B instead of the homopolymers A or C.

questions.explanation: This is a radical cyclisation through radical adddition to the C=C double bond. Once the radical is formed at the alpha carbon to the carbonyl group, it can react with the C=C bond. There are two possible products, a 5-membered and a 6-membered ring, depending on which carbon atom reacts with the radical. The exo cyclisation to form the 5-membered ring is the kinetically favoured pathway.

questions.question_text: Does one need to dry and degass the reaction glassware, solvent and reagents before performing a free radical reaction?
questions.explanation: Free radical reactions are not moisture sensitive, as water is not an active chemical in these reactions. However, O2 is a diradical, which can quickly react with any carbon-centred radical to form explosive peroxides and quench the free radicals, taking them out of the propagation steps. Thus, it is important to degass these reactions to ensure successful experiments.
